26 The variation with distance x of the intensity I along a stationary sound wave in air is shown.
I
0
0
5.0
10.0
15.0
x / cm
The speed of sound in air is 340 m s–1.
What is the frequency of the sound wave?
A
1700 Hz
B
2300 Hz
C
3400 Hz
D
6800 Hz

hints: Notice the intensity minima at $x = 5.0\text{ cm}$ and $x = 15.0\text{ cm}$ and measure their separation on the $x/\text{cm}$ axis.
Recall that intensity is proportional to (displacement amplitude)$^2$, so the $I$-$x$ pattern repeats twice as fast as the displacement stationary wave.
Connect the $10.0\text{ cm}$ separation of intensity minima to $\lambda/2$, then use $v = f\lambda$ with $v = 340\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Read the $I$ against $x$ graph: $I = 0$ at $x = 5.0\text{ cm}$ and again at $x = 15.0\text{ cm}$, with a maximum at $10.0\text{ cm}$ between them.
For a stationary wave, displacement amplitude varies as $\sin(2\pi x/\lambda)$, but intensity $I$ is proportional to amplitude squared, so $I$ varies as $\sin^2(2\pi x/\lambda)$.
A $\sin^2$ pattern has half the spatial period of the wave, so the distance between successive intensity minima is $\lambda/2$.
Use $v = f\lambda$ with $v = 340\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $f = 340/0.20 = 1700\text{ Hz}$.

B.explanation: 2300 Hz does not follow from $v = f\lambda$ with the correct $0.20\text{ m}$ wavelength from the $I$-$x$ graph.

C.explanation: 3400 Hz results from taking $10.0\text{ cm}$ as one full wavelength instead of half a wavelength for intensity.

D.explanation: 6800 Hz results from taking $5.0\text{ cm}$ as one full wavelength instead of a quarter wavelength for intensity.
